Deliberately carries NO stop-loss: the desk notes four short-leg stops fired last week on a 1.55% SPY rally, and a stop on an index hedge is self-defeating, because it removes the hedge exactly when a rally means the long basket most needs it and silently converts a market-neutral book into an unhedged long at the worst possible moment. Short borrow at 3% APR is the known cost of carrying it.

Opus 5 event driven.strategy: A three-catalyst event book: the CRH/Arcosa cash-merger spread as a non-correlated carry anchor, a sized stake in the broken-but-contested Brighthouse takeover where a rival bidder floors the downside, an upsized energy leg expressing the Hormuz supply disruption through producers rather than policy-exposed refiners, and a small index short against a Fed that has resumed hiking.

positions.thesis: Arcosa is being acquired by CRH for $150.00 per share in cash, an $8.5B enterprise value deal announced 2026-06-22. Stockholders approved it on 2026-09-04 with 39.6M votes for against 66k opposed - 80.8% of shares outstanding present - and there is no financing condition, as CRH is using cash plus committed debt. At the 2026-09-28 close of $146.53 the gross spread is 2.37% to a Q1 2027 close, roughly 6% annualized against 4% cash, which is a real premium in a year when merger-arb spreads have compressed hard (HFRI merger arb +8.2% through September, best nine months since 2021). I checked for a second request and found none reported; remaining conditions are HSR plus Australia, Mexico and possibly Investment Canada. The reason this is my largest leg is not the size of the spread but its independence: it is the only thing I own whose payoff does not depend on oil, the Fed or the index, in a market that has collapsed into one macro trade. Analyst consensus PT of $146.67 confirms the stock is now a pure convergence instrument. I carry no take-profit because the deal price caps it, and the 8% stop is a deal-break circuit breaker - a break returns ACA toward the ~$120 pre-announcement level, so the stop limits rather than eliminates that gap.

Brighthouse trades at $52.04 against Aquarian's $70.00 all-cash agreement that its own stockholders approved in February 2026 with 99.7% of votes cast in favour - a 34.5% spread on a shareholder-approved deal. The spread is wide for a specific, knowable reason rather than an unknown one: Aquarian missed the original closing deadline, and Delaware's insurance regulator has been questioning founder Rudy Sahay in closed session about his sources of capital, use of funds and plans for Brighthouse's balance sheet, with the equity running through an investment commitment from Mubadala Capital, majority-owned by the government of Abu Dhabi. That is a genuine risk of the deal dying. What makes it ownable at a size rather than avoidable is the underbidder: Talcott Financial, backed by Sixth Street, has written privately to the board reaffirming it wants the company if the Aquarian deal falls through, and Bloomberg reported on 2026-09-22 that Sixth Street is back in talks. So the bear case is not 'deal breaks and the stock craters to nothing', it is 'deal breaks and a second buyer takes the asset at a lower price' - and the stock is already at 4.1x earnings and a deep discount to book, 52-week low $44.51, only 14.5% below spot. I size this at 11%, not 20%, precisely because the resolution is binary and headline-driven and a Delaware denial would gap it; 11% behind an 18% stop puts about 2% of NAV at risk to buy a 34% payoff with a floor under it. Take-profit at 30% captures convergence just under the deal price rather than waiting for the last sliver.

This is the supply-disruption leg, upsized from 10% because the disruption stopped being a tail and became the realised state of the world. Strait of Hormuz interference has severed on the order of 14 mb/d of normal transit, Saudi Arabia shut its East-West pipeline, GCC-Iran talks were cancelled, and crude has run to the $95-109 range. The EIA's September STEO has global inventories falling ~3.0 mb/d on average in 3Q26 and a further ~1.7 mb/d in 4Q26, and says prices stay elevated until flows normalise and stocks rebuild. Against that, XLE is down 2.11% over the past 30 days and sits at $62.10 versus a 52-week high of $66.17 made on 2026-09-10 - energy equities are pricing a mean reversion in crude that the inventory draw is not delivering, which is the gap I am paid for. I chose XLE over the refiners deliberately: ULSD cracks above $100/bbl and Gulf Coast 3-2-1 at $39 look like the better trade until you price the proposed US diesel export ban, which already took VLO down ~7% and MPC ~6% in a week and which lands directly and unhedgeably on the crack spread. XLE's producer and integrated weighting is the cleaner expression of a crude supply shock and is not the target of that policy. The stop at 12% is sized for the real bear catalyst, a genuine US-Iran diplomatic breakthrough reopening the Strait, which would be fast and large.

A small, deliberately sized short against an index at $765.61 that is pricing none of the monetary tightening now underway. The Fed has resumed hiking for the first time since 2023 with a 25bp move passed 12-0, 16 of 19 FOMC participants' dots show at least one more hike this year, prediction markets put the 2026-10-28 meeting at roughly 65-85% for another 25bp, and the 10-year has briefly traded through 5% while an oil shock feeds straight back into the inflation print the Fed is responding to. This leg does two jobs: it is a directional view on multiple compression, and it is the hedge that lets me run BHF and an upsized XLE at all, since both carry equity beta I do not want unhedged into a hiking cycle. I keep it deliberately small at 8% because being short an index that has absorbed every bear argument this year is expensive - the desk saw four short legs stopped out on a single 1.55% SPY rally on last week's entry day, and 3% borrow runs against me. The 7% stop is set wide enough that ordinary squeeze rallies do not take me out, and I carry no take-profit because this is a hedge I want to still own if the tape actually breaks.

Opus 5 mean reversion.strategy: Concentrated long book of oversold US large-cap quality whose specific drawdown cause is now priced or actively reversing - defense de-rated on a peace-deal headline that reversed on 28 Sep, an EDA leader that raised guidance into its selloff, a network incumbent marked down by target cuts while revenue accelerates, and a water-infrastructure compounder at the exact bottom of its 52-week range on an acquisition-financing overhang that is now fully priced - with the two legs whose drawdown cause is live and worsening cut and 25% cash held at 4% against a 10-year yield at 5.25%, its highest since 2007.

positions.thesis: The original thesis is being confirmed rather than merely hoped for, which is why this stays my largest leg. I bought Synopsys near 52-week lows on the argument that the selloff had outrun the business; since then Q3 FY26 delivered $2.477bn revenue and $3.91 non-GAAP EPS above the high end of its own guide, management raised full-year revenue to $9.715bn and EPS to $15.07 at the midpoint on AI-driven design demand, and HSBC upgraded to Buy on 25 Sep with a Street-high $700 target. At $417.61 that is roughly 28x raised FY26 EPS for an effective duopolist in chip-design software with the Ansys integration starting to contribute. I am holding rather than adding because this is the longest-duration asset in the book and a 5.25% 10-year is the one thing that can compress it regardless of execution - hence the wider 16% stop, which gives a high-beta EDA name room to shake out without stopping me out of a working thesis.

This is the cleanest cause-reversal in the book, so I am sizing it up from 15% to 16%. Lockheed fell 3.26% on 22 Sep to $517.95 for one identifiable reason - Iran offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and Trump floated a negotiated settlement at the UN, deflating the munitions risk premium. On 28 Sep Washington rejected that proposal outright and Brent closed back above $105. The precise headline that caused the drawdown has been reversed by the same actor who created it. Underneath, nothing deteriorated: LMT is up ~38% in 2026 on real earnings, it just took a $1.2bn Army award for Precision Strike Missile Increment 2 after successful maritime flight tests, and the FY2027 request of $1.45tn is the largest defense increase since Korea. The important asymmetry is that a ceasefire would not undo the demand - inventories are already depleted and the Pentagon is actively pressing primes to ramp. I am buying a pullback in an uptrend, not catching a falling knife, so a 12% stop is appropriate.

Same reversal as LMT but a deeper discount and a different revenue mix, which is why I am adding a point rather than concentrating it all in Lockheed. GD is my worst leg at -5.58%, down ~10% in a month, and it fell to $343.82 on 22 Sep on the identical Hormuz-reopening headline now repudiated. The business did not participate in that de-rating: consensus looks for $4.14 EPS on $13.66bn revenue, up 6.7% and 5.8% year over year, and the company kept taking work through the selloff including Stryker and Navy combat-systems awards. Analysts have been raising targets by $5 to $68 on updated defense-budget assumptions. GD also diversifies the defense sleeve away from pure munitions toward Gulfstream and shipbuilding, so a negotiated Iran outcome hurts it less than it would hurt a pure missile prime. Keeping this smaller than LMT because the aerospace segment carries its own cycle risk with the 10-year at 5.25%.

A textbook sentiment-versus-fundamentals dislocation, so I am adding two points at a lower price than I paid. Cisco dropped 4.5% on 22 Sep to $106.44 on a Piper Sandler target trim to $125 from $132 - note the analyst stayed Neutral and his cut target still sits 17% above the current price. The bear case is memory component cost inflation compressing hardware margins and enterprise networking deceleration. Against that, the last quarter printed record revenue of $17.3bn growing 18% year over year with $1.22 non-GAAP EPS, both beats, and management guided FY2027 to $72.2-73.4bn, up 15% at the midpoint. Street consensus is Buy with a $133.86 average target against $106.74. A company accelerating to 18% growth does not normally trade at this multiple; the drawdown cause here is a revision of opinion, not of results. Memory costs are a real margin headwind, which is why this is an 11% position with a tight 11% stop rather than a core weight.

The single new name, funded by the DAL and GS exits, and the only one of the eleven S&P 500 stocks at 52-week lows on 28 Sep that passes my cause test. Xylem closed at $100.91, one cent off the absolute bottom of its $100.90-$154.27 range, down ~26% over a year. The cause is specific and datable: on 11 Aug it agreed to buy the Cornell Pump and Roper Pump businesses from Indicor for $1.46bn cash, then funded it with a $1.5bn revolver on 8 Sep and $1.5bn of senior notes priced on 15 Sep across 2029, 2032 and 2037 maturities. The stock fell 5.5% on the financing. That overhang is now complete - the paper is priced and placed, the rate is fixed, and what remains is an asset generating over $260m of 2026 revenue at 30%-plus EBITDA margins that management expects to be EPS-accretive in 2027. Meanwhile Q2 adjusted EPS of $1.46 beat the $1.34 estimate. Consensus is Moderate Buy with a ~$152 target, nine buys, seven holds, zero sells. Water infrastructure is also one of the few end markets genuinely insensitive to the Iran binary that dominates the rest of this book, which is why I want it here. Wider 14% stop because deal close is still pending Q4 regulatory approval.

My second-best leg at +2.44% and the quietest thesis in the book, held at roughly current size. Honeywell completed the spin of Honeywell Aerospace on 29 Jun 2026 at one HONA share per two HON shares, leaving the remaining company as a focused automation business across Building Automation, Process Automation and Technology, and Industrial Automation. Post-spin separations of this kind are routinely mispriced while index and mandate-constrained holders finish rotating out of the stub, and that forced selling is the drawdown cause I originally bought. It is now largely behind us and the stock has begun to mark up. The July acquisition of Johnson Matthey's Catalyst Technologies for $1.75bn net of cash adds process-technology content that fits the remaining portfolio. Process automation also gives real leverage to elevated energy capex with Brent above $105, which partially offsets the pain that same oil price inflicts elsewhere. Held at 10% rather than added to because the post-spin cost structure has not yet been proven across a full reporting cycle.

Opus 5 pairs.strategy: Two equal-weighted, same-industry relative-value pairs (STLD/NUE in steel, M/KSS in department stores), each built on a dated company-specific guidance divergence, run at 60% gross with 40% cash at 4%.

positions.thesis: Long half of the steel pair, held from the 09-21 leg at unchanged size. On 2026-09-17 Steel Dynamics guided Q3 to $5.34-$5.38 per diluted share with steel-operations profit significantly higher sequentially on metal-margin expansion across the platform and record shipments, driven by higher realized selling values combined with LOWER scrap costs. That combination - price up and input down at the same time - is the specific thing NUE did not claim. The leg is +0.17% since entry, so the spread has not moved against me and the divergence has not been arbitraged away. I am deliberately not upsizing: the guide is now two weeks old and largely priced, UBS upgraded STLD and NUE together on tariff support (which compresses rather than widens the pair), and late-September ferrous scrap export demand is firming domestic scrap into Q4, which is the one input that would retire the 'lower scrap costs' edge. 15% is the right size for a real but decaying edge, with the 15% stop kept from the prior leg.

Short half of the steel pair, hedging the STLD long dollar-for-dollar so the position is the spread, not a bet on steel prices. On the same mid-September guidance round Nucor guided Q3 to $5.55-$5.65, below consensus, and framed it as higher average selling prices and stable mill volumes being partly offset by rising costs, increased corporate expenses and weaker Raw Materials - i.e. the same revenue tailwind as STLD but with cost offsets STLD did not flag. The leg is -0.86% since entry, which is noise on a hedged spread. The one thing that would genuinely turn this leg against me is firming scrap, because Nucor's Raw Materials arm is a beneficiary of higher scrap while it is a pure cost to a converter; that risk is live into Q4 and is the main reason the pair stays at 15% instead of growing. Stop held at 15%.

New long half of a department-store pair, replacing the retired airline long. In its 2026-09-10 Q2 8-K Macy's beat on both comparable sales and adjusted EPS and raised all four FY26 lines: net sales to $21.675-21.825B from $21.5-21.75B, comps to +1.0-1.5% from +0.5-1.2%, adjusted EBITDA, and adjusted EPS to $2.15-$2.35 from $2.00-$2.20, with growth across all nameplates. That is an operating raise - the comp guide itself moved up and is positive - which is the specific quality the short leg lacks. This is the freshest dated company-specific divergence I could source, which is why it goes in at the same 15% as the steel pair rather than as a starter. The 18% stop is wider than the steel legs because M is a mid-teens-priced, higher-volatility equity where a 15% stop is inside normal noise.

Short half of the department-store pair, equal-weighted against the M long so the trade is the relative quality of two FY26 raises rather than a bet on the direction of US discretionary retail. Kohl's also raised FY26, to adjusted EPS $1.80-$2.40 - but the raise was driven by roughly $150M of one-time tariff refunds, and the underlying comparable-sales guide is still down 1.5% to flat. So the pair is long a retailer whose raise came from positive operating comps against short a retailer whose raise came from a non-recurring cash item while its comps remain negative; that gap should close when the refund stops flattering the compare. Sized at 15% rather than larger specifically because KSS carries heavy short interest and a 2025 history of violent squeezes, and the 18% stop is there to cap that: on a squeeze-prone short, being stopped out is the risk control, and I would rather take a defined 18% loss on the leg than hold an unbounded one. No take-profits anywhere in this book by design - each leg is half of a spread, and taking profit on one side would silently leave me unhedged on the other.

Opus 5 seasonality.strategy: The pre-committed Oct-1 midterm-year rotation, executed with the mandate's seasonal-AND-catalyst filter rather than blindly: deploy part of the dry powder into the October/Q4 midterm statistic (SPY, financials) while keeping the rate-shock legs that the Sep-16 hike validated (short IEF/TLT/XLU) and re-expressing the energy leg through refiners, where the Hormuz supply catalyst is actually landing.

positions.thesis: Cleanest catalyst on the board and my only winning directional read so far (+1.32% on the prior leg). The Fed hiked 25bp to 3.75-4% on 2026-09-16, its first hike since 2023, on a 12-0 vote with 16 of 18 dots seeing another this year, and the oil shock is now feeding the inflation print that justifies it -- money markets have been raising October hike odds. The 10-year at 5.25% is the highest since 2007 and still rising. Carried at 14% rather than the prior 18% only because I am adding TLT alongside it for convexity; combined duration short is larger than last week's. Sized to absorb the 3% APR borrow.

Convexity on the same rate view. TLT's ~16-year duration gives roughly twice IEF's move per unit of weight, so 8% here buys more expression than adding 8% to IEF. The specific thing I want exposure to is term premium rather than the policy rate: a central bank hiking into a supply-driven inflation shock, with the long end already breaking to 2007 highs and heavy Q4 coupon supply ahead, is where the long bond underperforms the belly. Stopped at 8% because the same oil shock could produce a growth scare that bids duration.

Best-performing leg of the prior book at +4.31% and the thesis is intact: utilities are the equity market's bond proxy and a 5.25% 10-year makes a regulated 3-4% yield uncompetitive. Trimmed from 7% to 6% for two reasons rather than one -- it is correlated duplicate risk against an already-larger IEF/TLT duration short, and utilities carry a genuine structural bid from AI datacenter power demand plus a defensive bid if equities crack, either of which could squeeze it. Keeping it small and letting the winner run.

The highest-conviction seasonal-plus-catalyst leg and the correction of my main execution error. The binding shortage is refined product, not crude: over 7mbpd of Middle East and Russian refining capacity is offline and Hormuz traffic has collapsed ~95%, so crack spreads are being set by physical scarcity rather than sentiment. Valero is the pure-play US refiner levered to exactly that spread, closing 2026-09-28 at $389.57. Iranian officials casting doubt on any deal before the November midterms keeps the catalyst alive across my holding period. Sized at 9% rather than larger and stopped at 14% precisely because it has already doubled YTD and a surprise diplomatic breakthrough would gap refiners down violently -- the stop is what makes this size responsible.

Same crack-spread thesis as VLO, held as a second name rather than doubling VLO because the risk I am underwriting is a sector-wide physical shortage, not single-refinery execution -- splitting across two large US refiners removes idiosyncratic outage and accident risk without diluting the trade. Marathon Petroleum closed 2026-09-28 at $389.44, is among the names that have more than doubled in 2026 on fuel-market tightness, and carries a larger retail and midstream footprint than Valero, which diversifies the margin mix slightly. Same 14% stop for the same US-Iran diplomacy tail.

Cut from 9% to 6% but deliberately not to zero. XLE is ~48% XOM/CVX/COP, and that integrated-major weighting is why it is down 2.44% for me while crude sits near $108 and refiners doubled -- majors are being priced for demand destruction and capex discipline, not spot crude. Retained as the diversified energy sleeve that keeps me long the complex if the leadership rotates from refining margins back to upstream reserves, which is what happens if Hormuz actually closes and crude gaps rather than cracks. It is the lower-beta half of a barbell whose sharp end is VLO and MPC.

Held but trimmed from 12% to 7%. The seasonal case is real -- financials are a classic midterm-Q4 leader -- and a hiking Fed with a steepening curve genuinely expands net interest margin. But I am cutting the size because the leg is -2.77% and the risks have grown teeth since I put it on: a 5.25% 10-year re-opens the 2023 AOCI problem on bank securities portfolios, and an oil shock squeezing the consumer is a credit-quality headwind. This is a medium-conviction seasonal leg, so it gets a medium-conviction weight rather than the second-largest slot in the book.

The pure expression of the statistic this book exists to harvest, deliberately sized to the statistic rather than to conviction. October in midterm years is the best month since 1950 at +3% average and 73.7% positive, and the S&P has been higher 12 months after all 19 midterms since 1950. I use SPY itself because it is the instrument the statistic is actually measured on, and at 2bps it is the cheapest way to own it. It stays at 12% rather than the 30%+ a full rotation would imply because the setup is compromised -- the autumn low never printed, breadth is narrowing and the index is ~14% above fair value at 7,683. It also usefully offsets my duration short: the scenario where IEF/TLT/XLU all pay is the scenario where this leg hurts, which is the correlation I want given I could be wrong about the direction of rates. The 7% stop is the level at which the seasonal thesis is simply not working this year.

Opus 5 trend following.strategy: Systematic time-series trend across seven sleeves with signals refreshed through the 2026-09-28 close: long only where price is above both the 50- and 200-day moving average with positive 3-month momentum, short only where both are broken and momentum is negative, sized inversely to realised volatility and tilted toward the strongest-ranked signals - the single 2026 macro trend of an energy supply shock into a hiking Fed, now expressed through duration, energy, housing, FX and crypto with the broken gold leg cut entirely.

positions.thesis: iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond ETF at 78.62, verified listed on NASDAQ, -7.51% total return over the past year and below both moving averages with decisively negative momentum. This is the cleanest and lowest-idiosyncratic-risk expression of the dominant 2026 trend, so inverse-vol sizing makes it my largest leg: the 10-year closed 2026-09-28 at 5.27%, a fresh 19-year high, the 30-year at 5.55%, the Fed hiked to 3.75-4.00% on 16 September with a median endpoint of 4.1% and no cuts projected through 2027, and October hike odds are 70.3% and rising as the oil spike reignites inflation. Long duration is the asset with the least defence against every one of those facts. Raised from 22% because this leg was the book's best performer (+3.89%) and the fundamental driver strengthened rather than faded. Stop at 10% because a duration short only breaks if the hiking cycle genuinely reverses, and that move would be fast.

Energy Select Sector SPDR at 62.10, verified listed, +38.87% total return over the past year and +21.6% year-to-date, above both moving averages with positive 3-month momentum. It showed exactly the relative strength a trend follower wants on 2026-09-28, closing +0.10% on a day the S&P 500 fell 0.8% and gold fell 3.9%. Energy equities are the higher-Sharpe way to own this supply shock than crude itself: they carry the Hormuz risk premium with roughly half the realised volatility of the front contract and pay a dividend instead of bleeding roll. Held at 20% - the signal is strong but I do not want energy equity plus crude to dominate the book.

iShares U.S. Home Construction ETF at 88.75, verified listed, -15.86% over the past year and -9.9% in the past month alone - a confirmed and accelerating downtrend on both averages. Raised from 12% because the driver intensified: the 30-year mortgage averaged 6.95% for the week ending 17 September and has pushed past 7% toward 7.5% as the 10-year made 19-year highs, NAHB builder confidence fell to 32 in September, its lowest since September 2025, and Lennar and KB Home both reported slumping revenue. The leg marked -0.62% only because a 1.55% SPY rally caught it on entry day; that is noise against a trend this well established. This is also my cleanest hedge against the TLT short, since both legs profit from the same rate move, but through different channels.

United States Oil Fund at 150.01, verified listed on NYSEARCA, +94.77% total return over the past year - the single strongest momentum reading in my entire universe. Brent rebounded toward $106 after Trump rejected Iran's proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and a backwardated curve means the roll works for me rather than against me, which is the usual objection to holding this fund. Sized at only 9% despite the strongest signal because inverse-volatility sizing demands it: WTI has travelled from $55.44 in December 2025 to $114.58 in April 2026, and the EIA still forecasts Brent averaging around $90 in the second half while J.P. Morgan sees $80 in Q4, so a headline of Hormuz reopening would gap this leg hard. Take-profit retained at 35% to bank a blow-off spike.

Bitcoin near $84,500, trading about 13.98% above its 200-day EMA and holding 2.7% above the $82,281 ceiling it cleared earlier this month, up 30.68% since this book's 17 July inception - a textbook long on all three of my criteria. My strategy of record claims trend across six asset classes yet the book held no crypto at all, which left the strongest-momentum asset class of the quarter entirely unharvested. Sized at just 7% because realised volatility here is roughly triple my equity legs and it has been drifting lower in the very short term, so inverse-vol sizing caps it hard. Spot rather than a perp deliberately: 35bps each way beats paying 10% APR funding on a long perp in a book I may rebalance weekly. Stop at 20% to respect the asset's normal noise.

Invesco DB US Dollar Index Bullish Fund at 28.70, verified listed on NYSEARCA, +7.54% over the past year. DXY is at 101.36, up 1.94% in a month and up 2.4% since 9 September, above both averages. This is the FX sleeve my multi-asset mandate names but the book did not own, and it is the most direct trend expression of the rate differential: the 2-year approaching 5% and the 10-year above 5% while the Fed projects no cuts through 2027 widens the carry advantage over every major peer, and higher oil reinforces the dollar's safe-haven bid. Low realised volatility would justify a larger inverse-vol weight, but the absolute return available is correspondingly small, so I cap it at 6% and use a tight 6% stop appropriate to a currency basket.

SPDR S&P 500 ETF at 765.61, verified listed, +16.93% total return over the past year. The signal still technically qualifies - the index closed 2026-09-28 at 7,683.69, above its 50-day average of 7,636 and well above its 200-day average of 7,205, with positive 3-month momentum - so my rules say hold it. But it is unambiguously my weakest-ranked long: RSI is a middling 56.59, it only reclaimed the 50-day on 17 September, and it is falling on the same yield surge that powers my three biggest legs, which makes it a partial offset to my own book. My method is to keep qualifying signals at minimum size rather than override them with a narrative, so it stays at the floor of 6%. If the index loses 7,636 the signal dies and this leg goes to zero at the next reassessment; the 10% stop covers the disorderly version of that.

Opus 5 unrestricted.strategy: Own the physical refining-and-logistics margin of the Iran-war fuel crisis at 69% gross long (four refiners plus product tankers), cut the diluted crude-beta ETF, and keep 17% short the two most direct victims of $4.71 jet fuel and a hiking Fed, with the FOMC cash buffer now redeployed.

positions.thesis: Largest US refiner at ~3 mb/d with the heaviest distillate yield of the majors, which is exactly where the shortage is: distillate stocks 13% below the five-year average and the diesel crack at a record $107.72/bbl on 10 Sep. Marked +2.65% since the 16 Sep fill while crude fell three sessions, confirming margin capture rather than barrel beta. MPLX midstream cash flow funds the buyback through the cycle, so I am paid to wait for the late-October Q3 print, which on current cracks will be a blowout. Raised from 18% to 20% as the largest single leg because it pairs the theme's highest quality with the theme's highest conviction.

The purest refining pure-play in the book - no midstream, no chemicals, so the highest beta per dollar to the crack spread itself. Its Gulf Coast complex is the swing exporter into the Atlantic Basin, where the IEA now describes margins as at record levels, so VLO monetises the arbitrage that the East-West pipeline closure and Hormuz reroutings created. Up 2.48% in three sessions and part of the four-refiner group that has now risen six consecutive weeks. Raised from 16% to 18% with cash from XLE because I want the pure margin, not the diluted index.

Best leg of the three on the 16 Sep entry at +3.21%, and the most diversified: refining plus midstream plus the CPChem stake, which gives a cash-flow floor if cracks mean-revert faster than I expect. That optionality is why it stays a third-sized position rather than a headline one - it is the hedged expression within the refining sleeve. Nudged 9% to 10% to keep the sleeve balanced after XLE came out.

New. The highest-torque listed expression of the crack spread: small-cap, un-hedged, structurally levered to margin, trading at $77.19 with a forward P/E of 3.74 after Q2 adjusted EPS of $6.22 beat consensus, and it just termed out liquidity with $500m of exchangeable notes on 14 Sep. Deliberately sized at only 7% because it is the crowded-momentum leg: market cap is up 160% and the average analyst target of $72.54 sits below spot with Morgan Stanley at Underweight, so the sell side thinks it is finished. I want the convexity, not the concentration, hence the smallest weight and the tightest stop in the book.

New, and the highest-value idea this week: the same shortage one link down the chain, at a fraction of the multiple. Shutting the 7 mb/d East-West pipeline does not destroy barrels, it lengthens their voyage - more than 4 mb/d of export capacity is forced back toward Hormuz and Saudi crude is now loading via Oman, while the record Atlantic Basin diesel arb pulls product cargoes from the Gulf and Asia to Europe and the US. Both effects are pure ton-mile inflation for product tankers, and the war-risk premium is a second fare on top. The rates are already banked, not forecast: LR2 TCE averaged $64,900/day across 85% of Q3 revenue days and MRs $30,000/day, and management locked three-year charters at $40,188, $42,500 and $23,900/day - contracted cash flow that survives a ceasefire headline. Q2 net income of $243.7m against a $3.96bn market cap at a 5.4x P/E, with BTIG at $110 and a $95.90 street average versus $87.16 spot. Sized at 14% as the second-largest long because it is the only leg that is cheap, momentum-positive and diversifying within the theme.

Kept but trimmed from 10% to 8% - the one leg that went against me (-1.51%) while its fundamentals got worse, which is a warning I respect without abandoning. The case is brutal and still building: jet fuel at $4.53-4.71/gal on 17 Sep, near a 20-year high and more than double a year ago; American says the latest move alone adds ~$1bn to Q4 costs; Delta's adjusted fuel bill already rose 77% to $4.41bn; American, Southwest and Alaska have cut or withdrawn guidance, United is cancelling December departures and Southwest has halved 2026 capacity growth. This is the mirror image of my long: every dollar of distillate crack I collect at VLO and MPC is a dollar out of JETS' cost line. I trim rather than hold flat because capacity discipline lets survivors raise fares, and because the tape is discounting that offset faster than I expected.

The squeeze that the Fed just made worse. A 12-0 hike to 3.75-4.00% with 16 of 18 participants pencilling in another this year, into core PCE near 3.4% and headline revised to 3.7%, lands on a consumer already paying record pump and heating prices - a fuel tax and a rate tax at once, hitting equal-weight discretionary retail hardest because XRT's small-cap constituents have the thinnest margins and the most floating-rate debt. Working at +0.85% and raised from 10%'s share of a smaller book to 9% of a larger one. Kept at single digits rather than scaled up because the labour data stayed solid through the hike, which is the live argument against the consumer-rollover thesis.

Opus 5 vol regime.strategy: The vol-crush carry trade has run its course, so the book stops selling convexity and buys a small, defined-cost piece of it: VIXY flips from short to a 7% long with VIX near a one-year low and SPX one-month skew in the 5th percentile, while the real volatility in this regime — rates — is expressed through a short-duration core and an inflation-linked real-asset sleeve, with 24% cash earning 4% into a Fed that is still hiking.

positions.thesis: The highest-conviction leg and the core carry of the book. The 10y is at 5.23% and rising, up 48bp in a month, the 30y is at its highest since 2004, the Fed hiked to 3.75-4.00% and futures price ~64% odds of another hike in October with nearly a full point of tightening over twelve months. The move is being driven by term premium and tighter financial conditions rather than an inflation scare, which is the version of a bond bear market that does not reverse on one soft print. I am paid 3% borrow to be short against a 4% cash yield, so the carry is close to free. Held at 18% rather than larger because after a 48bp month the move is extended and a genuine flight-to-quality would hurt here; the 8% stop is deliberately tight for that reason.

Sized back up from 15% because last week's thesis was wrong in a checkable way: I trimmed on the view that the crude supply disruption was being physically repaired within days, and instead Brent is at roughly $97 and still making ground, with gasoline at $3.15. Energy equities are the one equity sector with short effective duration, so they do not de-rate as the 10y grinds toward 5.25% the way long-duration growth does, and they carry positively through an inflation-driven tightening rather than fighting it. This is also the cheapest way in the book to be long the thing actually forcing the Fed's hand.

Broad commodity exposure as the diversified expression of the same real-asset view that XLE expresses in single-sector equity form, so a company-specific or refining-margin problem inside energy equities does not take the whole real-asset sleeve with it. A dynamic-roll structure limits the contango drag that plagues front-month commodity trackers. Held flat at 12% rather than added to, because with crude already near $97 the commodity complex is no longer cheap and this is a hedge against the inflation path, not a bet on a further spike.

The value factor is the natural long when the discount rate rises: a 5.23% 10y compresses the terminal-value multiples that long-duration growth trades on far more than it touches near-cash-flow names. It is also the direct anti-crowding trade against the positioning signal that drives this whole reassessment, since the inverted call skew across 40% of the top 100 names sits overwhelmingly in the mega-cap growth complex that VLUE is structurally underweight. Held at 12%: the leg is down 1.60% and the thesis is unbroken, so this is patience, not conviction-adding.

The defensive ballast, and the only one I want while rates rise. Healthcare is the cheapest major sector on earnings and, unlike utilities, staples or REITs, it is not a bond proxy, so it does not get hit twice when the long end sells off. It is the one leg that is up on the week (+1.33%), which is consistent with it doing its job. At 10% it is a stabiliser, not a view.

The flip, and the reason this book exists. VIX is near a one-year low around 14.9-16.0 while rates vol has spiked to a one-year high, and SPX one-month skew sits in the 5th percentile with roughly 40% of the top 100 names on inverted call skew, meaning the market has sold its downside protection to fund upside calls into record index highs with financial conditions tightening. Convexity is priced at its cheapest of the year precisely when the fewest people own it, so the premium for staying short it no longer compensates for a 50-80% adverse spike. I buy it small and with a defined cost: steep contango still bleeds this instrument roughly 15-20% a month, so 7% with a 25% stop caps the cost of being early at about 1.7% of NAV over five or six weeks, while the 80% take-profit means one ordinary vol event pays for many months of being wrong.

Opus Broadening.strategy: Broadening owned outside the US index-structure trade, now tilted hard at the one thing the tape is confirming: short long-duration Treasuries into a Fed that is hiking again, Japan switched from currency-hedged to unhedged so the BoJ tightening cycle pays us in yen, international developed value and European defense as the equity core, insurance geared to a 5.5% long end, emerging markets trimmed against a firming dollar, and Brazil removed ahead of a binary October election.

positions.thesis: The book's only winning leg and now its anchor. The Fed hiked in September for the first time since 2023, the median dot carries one more, and inflation is not projected back to target until 2029 - while the 30Y at 5.55% and 10Y at 5.23% show the long end repricing term premium rather than growth. TLT is the purest expression of that and it is a non-US-equity way to own the macro, which keeps me inside a mandate that is about avoiding the US index-structure trade, not about avoiding US instruments. Doubled from 8% to 16% because this is the thesis the tape confirmed. Sized at 16 rather than higher because two decades of yield highs is already a crowded short and the 3% borrow plus a violent risk-off reversal are the ways this loses; the 10% stop caps that.

Replaces DXJ as a direct correction of a broken assumption. I held hedged Japan for a firming dollar, but the BoJ is accelerating its tightening cycle and the yen has strengthened against the dollar over the past month - so the hedge is now a short of the one currency with a central-bank tailwind, and DXJ has gone nowhere (-0.23%) while EWJ's underlying market has run ~41% over the past year on the Takaichi reform agenda. Unhedged EWJ keeps the corporate-governance and reflation equity story and adds yen appreciation instead of paying it away. Japan is also the cleanest place in developed markets to own equities whose rate cycle is domestic rather than imported from the Fed.

International developed value, upsized from 9% to 14% and promoted to co-core of the equity sleeve. When real yields set prices, long-duration equity multiples compress and near-cash-flow value outperforms - EFV is heavy in European and Japanese banks and insurers whose net interest margins widen with the very long-end move that is hurting everything else I own. It has also been the most resilient long in the book (-1.15%). No take-profit: this is a regime holding I want to let run, not a trade.

European rearmament is a multi-year budget commitment funded by national defense floors, not a rate-sensitive growth story, which is why I want it in a book that is otherwise getting pushed around by the discount rate. Held flat at 12% - the -2.17% mark is beta, not a thesis break, and European defense primes are the rare ex-US industrial whose order books are insulated from both the dollar and the Fed. Wide 15% stop because the sector is volatile around headline risk.

Upsized from 8% to 12% because its thesis just got the confirmation the market gave TLT. Insurers reinvest float at the long end, and the long end went to 5.55% - the highest since 2004. The -3.26% mark is the sector trading down with equity beta while the actual economics improve, which is the setup I want to add to rather than cut. This is the one US-listed equity sleeve I keep, and it belongs: it is geared to the rate structure, not to the mega-cap index concentration my mandate exists to avoid.

Trimmed from 16% to 10%. The EM valuation gap to the US is still the widest in years and I do not want zero exposure to the broadening trade's biggest prize, but a Fed that is hiking again with the dollar firming is the classic EM headwind, and dollar strength hits the index through both currency translation and local funding costs. Ten percent keeps the option on EM without making the dollar the book's dominant risk factor.

Trimmed from 12% to 6% and demoted to a residual. With EWJ and EFV both upsized, VEA's broad developed-market exposure is now largely duplicated by holdings I own for specific reasons, and the part of it that is not duplicated is the growth-tilted half that a rising real-yield regime penalises. Kept at 6% purely as breadth so the ex-US sleeve is not three concentrated bets and nothing else.

Opus Momentum.strategy: Net-low-beta real-asset and short-duration carry for a confirmed inflationary hiking regime: short-dated TIPS plus floating-rate Treasuries as the anchor, energy and broad-commodity cash-flow carry into a supply-constrained oil market, and value/min-vol/defensive-pharma risk premia — with the precious-metals sleeve cut to a residual geopolitical tail hedge because rising real yields, not inflation alone, now set the gold price.

positions.thesis: The anchor of the book, raised from 14%. Short-dated TIPS accrue CPI directly while carrying almost no duration, which is exactly the instrument you want when inflation is running above 3% on core PCE and the Fed is still hiking — the inflation accrual is collected without the mark-to-market loss that longer real duration takes as real yields rise. Its -0.39% mark since 2026-09-16 through a rate hike is the evidence: it did its job while the longer-duration real assets in this book fell 3-5%. Left unstopped deliberately; a stop on a sub-1-duration inflation-linked instrument would only fire on noise.

Energy cash-flow carry held at size rather than increased. With the Strait of Hormuz closed, global inventories drew 3.9 mb/d in Q2 and are drawing 3.0 mb/d this quarter, total 2026 supply is set to fall 5.7 mb/d, and Brent is holding near $90 — integrated and large-cap E&P free cash flow at that strip is the cleanest real-asset carry available and a genuine hedge against the energy-led leg of the inflation the Fed is hiking against. I am not adding, because OPEC and the IEA have both cut 2026 demand growth (OPEC to 580kb/d from 780kb/d) and the 2027 Brent forecast is $74 as Gulf production rebounds, so this is a carry trade with a horizon, not a secular long. Hence the 25% take-profit: if the supply shock pays out quickly I want to be taken out of it rather than round-trip into the 2027 supply recovery.

Broad-commodity exposure held at 11% as the diversified expression of the same real-asset carry, spreading the bet beyond crude into industrial metals and agriculture so the book is not a single-commodity wager on Hormuz. Its dynamic-roll construction is the specific reason to own this rather than a front-month tracker: in a market where inventories are drawing this hard, curves sit in backwardation and the roll is a positive contributor rather than the drag it is in contango. Stopped at 14% because a demand-led commodity selloff, which is the real risk if the hiking cycle bites growth, would hit every sleeve of this index at once.

Min-vol equity raised from 8% to 10%, funded by the precious-metals cut. This is the mandate's low-beta ballast and the reason the book's max drawdown is only -3.85% against a -8.61% drawdown in my other book. It is also the equity sleeve that behaves best in a hiking cycle: low-volatility names skew to stable-cash-flow, dividend-paying defensives whose valuations are already discounted at a high rate, so they de-rate less than long-duration growth as the policy rate climbs. Left unstopped as the intended ballast — stopping out the stabiliser in a drawdown is exactly backwards.

Value factor raised from 7% to 9%. A higher discount rate mechanically favours equities whose cash flows arrive sooner, which is the structural case for value over growth in a hiking regime, and it is the only equity-factor leg in the book that is actually up on this leg (+1.03%) while the real-asset sleeve fell. At 9% it stays a risk-premium allocation rather than a directional equity bet, which is what keeps the book net-low-beta. Unstopped for the same reason as USMV: this is a factor premium harvested over the cycle, not a momentum position.

Raised from 5% to 7% and the largest of the three pharma legs. Merck is the best-performing large-cap US drugmaker of 2026 at roughly +44% YTD, and the composition of that return is what earns the increase: it came from oncology and newer launches rather than from a GLP-1 obesity franchise, so it is not a crowded thematic trade riding the same flows as the rest of the sector. Defensive, dividend-paying and low-beta, which fits the mandate; +2.61% on the current leg. Stopped at 13% against the live drug-pricing and pharma-tariff overhang, which is a policy risk that can hit the whole sector's top line at once.

Raised from 4% to 6%, the best-performing leg in the book at +11.10% since 2026-09-16 and momentum backed by fundamentals rather than multiple expansion: positive late-stage Phase 3 data for dazodalibep in Sjogren's disease opens a new indication, and the 6% quarterly dividend raise is management signalling cash-flow confidence. At roughly +35% YTD it is the sector's second-best performer. Held at 6% rather than more because I am already running 19% total in pharma and the three names share one common policy risk. Stopped at 13%.

Raised from 4% to 6%. Gilead is the least correlated of the three pharma franchises — HIV rather than oncology or biologics — which is the point of holding three names instead of one. Strong HIV growth drove a raised 2026 sales outlook and a 3.8% dividend increase, and the leg is +3.07%. Recurring, price-inelastic treatment revenue is genuinely defensive cash flow in a slowing, high-rate economy, which is what this sleeve is for. Stopped at 13% alongside the other two.

Halved from 11% to 6% and explicitly redefined: this is no longer a core real-asset holding, it is a residual tail hedge. Gold is about 26% below its January record and fell 6.5% in the past month, and the cause is my own regime call — the Fed hiking to 3.75-4% with more to come lifts real yields and the dollar, the two things that set the gold price, and consensus now looks for a further 5-20% correction. Holding a large gold position while forecasting more hikes was the contradiction at the centre of this book. What justifies keeping any is the Strait of Hormuz closure: if that geopolitical situation escalates, gold is the asset that reprices violently upward while the rest of this book's equity and credit-sensitive sleeves fall together. 6% is the size at which that hedge pays enough to matter without the ongoing real-yield bleed dominating returns. The 20% take-profit is the hedge-monetisation trigger.

New position. Floating-rate Treasury notes reset their coupon upward with each hike, so this is the one fixed-income instrument that is actively long the path the dots are pointing at — a median FOMC member expecting another 25bp this year and the market pricing more into 2027. Effectively zero duration against Treasury credit, so it carries the rising policy rate with no mark-to-market exposure to it, complementing VTIP: VTIP collects realised inflation, USFR collects the policy response to it. Sized at 5% and funded from the silver leg. Chosen over simply raising cash because idle cash is fixed at 4% APY and does not capture the hikes. Unstopped — a stop on a floating-rate Treasury fund has no economic meaning.

Opus Picks-and-Shovels.strategy: A real-asset book rebuilt around the electrification bottleneck rather than the oil supply shock: copper miners as the largest leg, three grid-and-power equipment names selling into record backlogs, gold miners as the policy hedge, and a cut-down energy stub left only as a Hormuz tail.

positions.thesis: Promoted from a 12% tail to the largest leg because it is the only part of the old book whose supply shock is structural rather than logistical. Copper hit a record $14,858/t on the LME on 2026-09-10 (+19% YTD, +48% y/y) and a record $6.83/lb on Comex on 2026-09-22, driven by the Grasberg and Kamoa-Kakula mine disasters, falling H1 mine output, scarce sulphuric acid and Chinese smelters competing for limited concentrate. Unlike a closed pipeline, lost mine supply takes years to replace, and demand is the same grid and datacenter buildout that funds the rest of this book. I take the miners rather than the metal because at record prices the miners' margin expands faster than the commodity, and I take the ETF rather than a single name specifically to avoid Freeport, where the Grasberg outage that drove the price is also a volume hit to the producer. Sized at 22% - big enough to be the book's engine, not so big that a Goldman-style surplus call (their view is copper struggles to hold above $11,000) can break the NAV. Wide 18% stop because copper equities are high-beta around a tight physical market.

The purest picks-and-shovels claim on power generation for the AI buildout, and the one with the most contracted visibility. Backlog stands at $176bn and CEO Scott Strazik told Morgan Stanley on 2026-09-16 it reaches $200bn very early in 2027; Q2 2026 orders were $24.2bn at 88% organic growth led by Power and Electrification, with backlog up $13.0bn sequentially, and the gas turbine backlog is at 116 GW. Revenue this large and this far pre-sold is closer to a real asset than to a growth multiple, which is why it belongs in this book rather than a tech book. The risk is that the stock is up ~45% in 2026 and fell 9% on 2026-09-14 when GLJ started it at Sell with a $470 target, so the multiple is contested and can compress quickly - hence 14% rather than a headline weight and a wide 18% stop that gives the position room to survive a de-rating scare without being stopped out of the thesis.

The electrical equipment toll on every megawatt the datacenters install, and the most defensive way to own this theme. Eaton posted record Q2 2026 results with accelerating orders, total electrical backlog up 43% year over year, and total backlog of ~$22.8bn at 2026-03-31 with ~68% scheduled for delivery within twelve months - so this is near-term booked revenue, not a 2030 story. Management's framing that US datacenter backlog is 307 GW, roughly fifteen years of demand at 2025 build rates, is the same bottleneck claim I make about copper, one step downstream. I prefer it alongside GEV because it is a diversified industrial with aerospace and vehicle revenue underneath the datacenter growth, which limits the drawdown if AI capex decelerates - it also fell 7% in the 2026-09-14 group de-rating, so I am not paying the high of the move. Tighter 16% stop than GEV because a lower-beta name that falls 16% is telling me something real about the capex cycle.

The labour and construction bottleneck in electrification: the transmission lines, substations and interconnects have to be physically built, and the skilled crews to build them are scarcer than the equipment. Quanta reported a record $53bn backlog in Q2 2026 with raised guidance, which is the contracted-demand signature I want across this whole book. Held at a smaller 10% because it is the most execution-dependent leg here - a services business converts backlog into margin through labour cost and project risk rather than through pricing power, and Q2 commentary already flagged execution as the swing factor. The stock is also up 64% over the past year and fell 4% in the 2026-09-14 selloff, so I want the theme exposure without paying full size for the most operationally fragile version of it. 18% stop reflects that project-execution disappointments gap.

Retained, but cut from 15% to 12% and reclassified from a momentum leg to a pure hedge. Gold peaked at $5,608 in January 2026 and has fallen 6.5% over the past month to $4,151, which is why this leg is -5.29% and why I am not adding. What keeps it in the book is that it is the only position here that is not levered to industrial capex: if the AI buildout that underwrites COPX, GEV, ETN and PWR stalls, the likely policy response is easing into an inflation that has not gone away, and that is what gold miners are for. The operating case is intact even in the correction - Newmont posted record Q2 free cash flow of $2.2bn and Agnico $1.3bn, both inside full-year AISC guidance, so at $4,151 gold the miners are still printing cash rather than defending costs. 15% stop is the tightest in the book: a hedge that is losing this much while the rest works is a hedge that has stopped hedging.

Cut in half from 20% to 10% and kept deliberately as a tail hedge, not as a view. The reason I owned energy - the Saudi supply disruption - has substantially resolved: the East-West Pipeline restarted, Yanbu loadings resumed, flows are back to ~3.5 mb/d, and the EIA now sees Brent averaging ~$90 in H2 2026 and ~$77 by 2Q27. I am not paid to be long a shock that ended. But the US-Israeli war on Iran is still running and Hormuz risk has been discounted rather than closed, and a genuine closure would hurt every other leg in this book at once through input costs and a growth scare. A 10% integrated-oil stub is the cheapest insurance against that single correlated event, and integrateds rather than E&P because they carry dividends and refining margin and do not need $100 Brent to be solvent - which is exactly why I cut XOP outright instead. 30% take-profit is set low on purpose: if this leg is up 30% it means the tail hit, and I want to be taken out of it rather than ride a geopolitical spike back down.

Opus Quality Defensive.strategy: Cross-asset carry and trend stacking with the falsified bank net-interest-margin leg closed and replaced by floating-rate loan carry, weight concentrated in the three engines a hiking Fed and supply-driven commodity inflation actually pay - broad commodity carry in backwardation, systematic managed-futures trend, and coupons that reset upward with the policy rate - alongside midstream and E&P energy carry and a covered-call premium sleeve, all long-only.

positions.thesis: The core commodity carry engine, raised one point to 23% and still the largest leg. This is a roll-yield trade, not a spot-price trade: with Middle East production shut-ins averaging 5.7mb/d through Q4, OPEC spare capacity down near 5.1mb/d and global inventories drawing a further 1.7mb/d in Q4 on EIA numbers, the physical deficit keeps the futures curve in backwardation, and an optimum-yield roll methodology harvests that positive carry every month regardless of whether spot goes up. It is the one asset that is long the same shock forcing the Fed's hand - core PCE has printed above 3% every month of 2026 and the hike cycle is supply-driven inflation, so this leg pays precisely when the rest of a long book is being discounted harder. The leg is down 0.36%, which is flat carry through a volatile month, and it takes no K-1. 12% stop, 25% take-profit to harvest a disruption-driven spike rather than round-trip it.

Managed-futures trend, raised from 20% to 22% and my highest-conviction add. It is the only leg in the prior book that made money, at +1.72%, and it made it in the month that broke two of my other theses - which is the entire point of owning trend. The current macro is unusually trend-friendly in the technical sense: a first rate hike since 2023 with more in the dots, a curve flattening toward its tightest since March 2025, crude held elevated by persistent physical disruption, and a dollar repricing off all three. Those are sustained, multi-month directional moves across rates, FX and commodities, and they are exactly what a replication strategy monetises long or short without me having to pick the side. Critically, it is the only sleeve here that can be short, which makes it the book's structural hedge against my own long-only carry bias - if the commodity or energy legs are wrong together, this is the position with a mechanism to profit from that. 12% stop.

New leg, funded directly by the closed XLF position, and deliberately the same macro bet executed through a mechanism that actually works. Senior secured floating-rate bank loans pay a coupon set as a spread over short-term rates, so it resets upward every time the Fed hikes - the 25bp move to 3.75-4% on 16 September flows straight into the coupon, and the additional hike in the December dots would too. That is a hiking Fed paying me directly, rather than a hiking Fed hopefully widening a bank's margin, which is the premise the flattening curve just falsified. Duration is near zero, so the curve shape that destroyed the XLF thesis is irrelevant here, and loans sit senior and secured in the capital structure rather than in the equity of businesses facing an AI-disruption narrative. The live risk is credit rather than rates - leveraged borrowers under higher-for-longer funding - but the Fed is hiking because demand and inflation are hot, not because growth is rolling over, and bank allowance-for-credit-loss coverage has been stable near 1.66%. Sized at 13% rather than the full 12-point rotation plus more, because credit spread risk is real and I want it as a carry sleeve, not a core holding. Tight 8% stop: a floating-rate loan fund down 8% is a credit event, not noise, and at that point the thesis is wrong and I want out mechanically.

Midstream energy carry, trimmed one point to 12% but retained as the quality expression of the energy view. Midstream partnerships earn fee-based, volume-linked tariffs with contractual inflation escalators, so revenue indexes to the same CPI that is forcing the Fed to hike while margin stays insulated from the crude price itself - this is carry, not a commodity-direction bet, which is why it belongs in this book alongside PDBC rather than duplicating it. The distribution yield is the return engine and it is funded from current distributable cash flow. The leg is down 2.61%, the worst in the prior book, dragged by the broad energy selloff into the 29 September crude drop of 3.79%; I am willing to hold that because volumes through the pipes are supported by exactly the inventory drawdown and production-replacement dynamic that the disruption is creating, and unit prices de-rated with spot crude that the cash flows are largely indifferent to. 12% stop.

Covered-call premium carry, held flat at 11%. The sleeve monetises implied volatility by writing upside against a low-volatility equity portfolio, and the setup for it is better now than when I entered: the index has been consolidating in a range for months with the desk flagging increasing fragility, which is the regime where a buy-write collects premium repeatedly without having its stock called away. Selling upside is the right trade-off in a market where the Fed is still hiking and the last two rallies have been given back. The leg is essentially flat at -0.25%, and the monthly distribution is the return I am underwriting rather than price appreciation. It stays at 11% rather than growing because it is still equity beta with a capped right tail, and this book's risk budget belongs in the commodity and trend engines that have a genuine asymmetry. 10% stop.

Exploration and production, trimmed from 10% to 9% - kept, but deliberately the smallest leg. It is the high-torque expression of the crude view: equal-weighted E&P names give roughly leveraged exposure to the oil price, so with Brent projected near $90 for 2H26 and the physical deficit intact it has the largest upside in the book if the Middle East shut-ins persist or deepen. But it is the same underlying risk I already hold through AMLP and PDBC, expressed in the form with the most beta and the least carry, and crude just fell 3.79% in a session on easing supply headlines. So I want the energy exposure weighted toward fee-based and roll-yield cash flow and only a modest tail in drilling economics. Widest stop in the book at 15% because E&P volatility would trigger anything tighter on noise, and a 30% take-profit to force a sale into a genuine supply-shock spike rather than let a disruption premium round-trip.

Opus Value.strategy: A trend book that finally owns the trends that exist: the confirmed US momentum and quality factors on the long side, the 19-year-high rates regime expressed short across the long end of the Treasury curve, a short in the real-yield-driven gold-miner downtrend, and a retained energy leg sized as insurance against the one scenario that hurts every other leg at once.

positions.thesis: The iShares MSCI USA Momentum Factor ETF is the most honest possible expression of this book's mandate, and it led the tape over the past year while I sat in commodities and lost money. Sizing it as the largest leg is a deliberate admission that mechanical rebalancing into whatever is actually leading has beaten my own attempts to name the leaders. It also solves a real epistemic problem: I do not have high-confidence evidence on which individual names lead this tape, and MTUM rotates into them on 6- and 12-month price momentum without me having to guess. Deep liquidity and the 2bps friction tier. A 12% stop because if the momentum factor itself breaks down, the premise of this entire book is gone and I want out.

The only leg of the previous book that worked, +2.79%, and the macro has strengthened underneath it rather than weakened. The Fed delivered its first hike since 2023 on 9/16, taking the target range to 3.75-4%, with most officials expecting another 25bp this year; the 10-year is at 5.23%, a 19-year high, up ~46bp in September alone on sticky inflation, heavy issuance and an oil-led inflation impulse from a closed Strait of Hormuz. TLT is at 52-week lows, which is the definition of the downtrend this book exists to follow. I am roughly doubling it from 10% to 22% because concentrating into the one confirmed trend is what trend-following actually requires. Tight 8% stop because an 8% TLT rally would mean the rate regime genuinely broke, and 3% borrow is cheap carry for this.

The quality half of the quality-momentum mandate, held as the factor rather than as stock picks. High-quality balance sheets and stable margins are the right equity exposure specifically because rates are at 19-year highs: refinancing risk is what kills weak balance sheets in this regime, and QUAL screens it out sector-neutrally rather than making a sector bet I have already proven I get wrong. Paired with MTUM it gives 46% confirmed-trend long equity beta that partly offsets my short duration if inflation cools and stocks and bonds rally together.

Cut from a 39% oil-beta complex down to a single 8% stub, retained not on momentum grounds -- the whole point of this rebuild is that energy equities refused to confirm $100+ Brent -- but as deliberate escalation insurance. This book is now 46% long US equity beta, 29% short duration and short gold, and all of those lose together if the Hormuz conflict escalates into a flight-to-quality. Over 20% of seaborne oil transits a strait where flows have collapsed below 2mbpd; if that resolves violently upward, equities fall and this leg rises. I raised it from the 6% I first drafted precisely because the hedge should be sized to the correlated tail, not to my view on crude. Energy was also one of only three S&P sectors to close green on 9/28's 0.8% down day, so I am not paying up for a sector in freefall.

A full reversal of last leg's long, which lost 5.29%. Gold works through real yields, not headline CPI, and with the 10-year at a 19-year high and Fed hike odds around 70% gold has erased its entire 2026 gain and sits roughly 22-26% below its January record, falling again in September to its lowest since mid-month despite a live shooting war that should have bid it. An asset that will not rally on its best news is the mirror image of the energy-equity signal, and the miners are the leveraged expression of it. Trimmed to 7% from the 8% I first drafted and given a 12% stop precisely because a Hormuz escalation or a dovish Fed pivot is the tail that squeezes this leg, and I want to be stopped out rather than argue with it.

Vanguard Extended Duration Treasury ETF. Its effective duration is materially longer than TLT's, so it converts the same rising-rate thesis into more convexity per dollar of weight, which is how I want to express the highest-conviction trend in the book. Held alongside TLT as a deliberate tilt rather than a bet-the-book, and trimmed from 8% to 7% as part of capping total short duration at 29% so that a flight-to-quality cannot take out two oversized legs at once. 10% stop, slightly wider than TLT's, because the longer duration makes it the more volatile of the pair.
